metadata.title: Department of Army v. Blue Fox, Inc., 525 U.S. 255 (1999) (No. 97-1642)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Department of Army v. Blue Fox, Inc.

Opinion filed: 1999-01-20

Docket No.: 97-1642

Citations:
• 142 L. Ed. 2d 718
• 119 S. Ct. 687
• 525 U.S. 255
• 1999 U.S. LEXIS 746

Case holding summaries:
• “Bowen held that Congress employed this language [‘money dam- ages’] to distinguish between specific relief and compensa- tory, or substitute, relief.”
• “Damages are given to the plaintiff to substitute for a suffered loss, whereas specific remedies ‘are not substitute remedies at all, but attempt to give the plaintiff the very thing to which he was entitled.’” (emphasis in original
• holding that action for lien seeks “money damages” because “its goal is to seize or attach money in the hands of the Government as compensation . . .”
• stating the APA waives the government’s sovereign im- munity from actions seeking relief other than monetary damages
• statutes abrogating sovereign immunity are to be strictly construed
• interpreting scope of the federal government's waiver of sovereign immunity under the APA
• “Absent a waiver, sovereign immunity shields the Federal Government and its agencies from suit.” (quoting FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471, 475 (1994))
• The Supreme Court has "frequently held . . . that a waiver of sovereign immunity is to be strictly construed, in terms of its scope, in favor of the sovereign" and that "[s]uch a waiver must be `unequivocally expressed' in the statutory text."
• describing the nature of an equitable lien
• §702 does not cover claims that seek a financial substitute for the legally required performance by the agency
• statutes abrogating sovereign immunity are to be strictly construed
• instructing that "[w]aiver of the federal government's sovereign immunity must be expressed in unequivocal statutory text and cannot be implied"
• “We have frequently held . . . that a waiver of sovereign immunity is to be strictly construed, in terms of its scope, in favor of the sovereign.”
• holding that sovereign immunity barred subcontractor's equitable lien against United States
• describing Section 702 as waiving the Government's immunity from actions seeking relief other than money damages
• "We have frequently held, however, that a waiver of sovereign immunity is to be strictly construed, in terms of its scope, in favor of the sovereign. Such a waiver must also be 'unequivocally expressed in the statutory text.'"
• "`Absent a waiver, sovereign immunity shields the Federal Government and its agencies from suit.'" (quoting FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471, 475, 114 S.Ct. 996, 127 L.Ed.2d 308 (1994))
• holding that sovereign immunity bars an APA claim for money damages even when pursued as an equitable remedy
• Section 702 makes distinction between specific relief and substitute relief, not equitable and nonequitable categories of remedies
• noting that "sovereign immunity bars creditors from attaching or garnishing funds in the Treasury, or enforcing liens against property owned by the United States" (citations omitted)
• "An equitable lien ... merely grants a plaintiff 'a security interest in the property, which [the plaintiff] can then use to satisfy a money claim' " (quoting Dan B. Dobbs, Law of Remedies s 4.3(3), at 601 (2d ed. 1993))
• " Bowen's interpretation of § 702... hinged on the distinction between specific relief and substitute relief, not between equitable and nonequitable categories of remedies."
• stating that "the laborers and materialmen had a right to be paid out of the fund [retained by the Government]" and hence a surety was subrogated to this right
• "As against the United States, no lien can be provided upon its public buildings or grounds"
